chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil and Muhammad ibn Humran, that they asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the sacrifices of the Jews, Christians, and Magians, so he said:

"Eat [them]." Some of them said, "Indeed, they do not mention [God's name]." He said, "If you are present with them and they do not mention [God's name], then do not eat [them]." And he said, "If they are absent [of your presence], then eat [them]."
ai.seo_question: When is the meat of the People of the Book considered halal according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This ruling from Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) establishes the principle of *istishab* (presumption of permissibility) for the meat of the People of the Book, distinguishing between explicit doubt and absence of evidence. In Shia jurisprudence, this hadith is pivotal in debates regarding whether 'eating' implies 'slaughtering in the name of God' or merely 'mentioning it,' with the Imam clarifying that absence of the name during absence of the Muslim renders it permissible, while presence with omission renders it impermissible. This nuanced distinction highlights the Shia emphasis on contextual verification (*takhassus*) over blanket prohibitions found in some Sunni schools.
